dt6_how_it_counts.topic: How instant-runoff ranked-choice voting counts, with NYC and Maine worked cases

claims.text: NYC 2021 Democratic mayoral primary round 1: Adams 289,403 (30.7%), Wiley 201,127 (21.4%), Garcia 184,463 (19.6%), Yang 115,130 (12.2%); 8 rounds; final Adams 404,513 (50.4%) vs Garcia 397,316 (49.6%), margin 7,197; 140,202 inactive ballots in the final round

NYC 2025 Democratic mayoral primary round 1: Mamdani 469,642 (43.8%), Cuomo 387,137 (36.1%), Lander 120,634 (11.3%); 3 rounds; final Mamdani 573,169 (56.4%) vs Cuomo 443,229 (43.6%); 55,332 inactive in final round

Maine 2nd District 2018 round 1: Poliquin 134,184 (46.3%), Golden 132,013 (45.6%), Bond 16,552 (5.7%), Hoar 6,875 (2.4%); final Golden 142,440 (50.6%) vs Poliquin 138,931; 8,253 exhausted of 289,624; Poliquin sued 13 Nov 2018 and asked to end the recount 14 Dec 2018
Fair Representation Act text sets ranked-choice counting rules for single-seat and multi-seat races, ties resolved by lot, and $4-$8 per registered voter federal payments for implementation

dt6_where_it_runs.topic: Where RCV runs and where it is banned: NYC, Maine, Alaska, bans, 2024 ballot record, 2026 measures

claims.text: NYC charter amendment 5 Nov 2019: yes 510,153 (73.61%), no 182,900; RCV for primaries and specials for mayor, public advocate, comptroller, borough president, council from 2021; up to five ranks

NYC 2025 (FairVote report): SurveyUSA found 96% said ballot simple, 81% understand RCV extremely or very well, 76% want to keep or expand; ballot data show 78% ranked at least two in the Democratic mayoral primary; 5.6% of votes inactive in RCV-tabulated contests; mayoral primary turnout 34.6%

Maine Question 5 passed 52.12-47.88 on 8 Nov 2016; 23 May 2017 the Supreme Judicial Court unanimously advised RCV conflicts with the constitution's plurality rule for governor and legislature general elections; 12 June 2018 voters approved a people's veto overturning LD 1646 (the delay law)

Baber v. Dunlap, 13 Dec 2018 (Walker, J.): Maine's RCV Act as applied to the 2018 2nd District race violated neither the Constitution nor federal law; Article I 'perfectly silent' on how states elect representatives; 'The Constitution does not require an easy ballot'

Alaska 2020 Measure 2 passed 174,032 (50.55%) to 170,251 (top-four primary, RCV general, 'true source' disclosure), upheld by state supreme court 19 Jan 2022; 2024 repeal failed 160,230 (49.88%) to 160,973, narrowest in state history; 2026 Measure 2 on 3 Nov 2026 ballot, 42,837 signatures verified 31 Dec 2025, supreme court ordered added language 27 Aug 2026; backers include Trump, Rep. Begich, Gov. Dunleavy, Alaska GOP, Musk; opponents include AFL-CIO, Libertarian Party, Unite America; through 2 Oct 2026 support raised $2.52M, opposition $8.55M (Unite America PAC $4.87M)

Alaska Aug 2022 special: round 1 Peltola 75,799 (40.19%), Palin 58,973 (31.27%), Begich 53,810 (28.53%); Begich ballots 27,053 to Palin, 15,467 to Peltola, 11,290 exhausted; Peltola 91,266 (51.48%) to 86,026; 48.40% of round-1 ballots; head-to-head Begich beat Palin ~61.41% and Peltola ~52.51% (Condorcet winner eliminated first); monotonicity and no-show paradoxes also present
RCV bans by July 2024: 2022 Florida, Tennessee; 2023 Idaho, Montana, South Dakota; 2024 Alabama, Kentucky, Louisiana, Mississippi, Oklahoma; Missouri vote pending

2025 bans: Arkansas, Iowa (signed 2 June 2025), Kansas, North Dakota, West Virginia, Wyoming; 17 total; all but two under Republican trifectas, Kansas and Kentucky under divided government (Republican legislature, Democratic governor)
Indiana's ban signed 24 Feb 2026 by Gov. Braun; 18 states ban RCV (count corrected from 19 after Utah's pilot expired 1 Jan 2026)

2024: DC Initiative 83 (establish RCV) 73% yes, Missouri Amendment 7 (ban) 68% yes, both approved; defeated: Montana CI-126 49%, Alaska repeal 49.9%, Nevada Q3 47%, Colorado 131 46%, Oregon 117 42%, Arizona 140 41%, Montana CI-127 40%, South Dakota H 34%, Idaho Prop 1 30%

RCV in Nov 2026: Alaska and Maine, DC, 11 cities (Albany, Berkeley, Oakland, San Francisco, San Leandro, Boulder, Arden, Portland ME, Takoma Park, Corvallis, Portland OR) and 2 counties (Multnomah, Arlington); Honolulu, Irvine and Longmont vote on adoption 3 Nov 2026

dt6_the_critics.topic: The research and critiques of RCV: exhaustion, majorities, confusion, turnout, Condorcet failure; proportional representation

claims.text: New America review of 15 studies: initial confusion largely faded after a second RCV round; voters penalized candidates of color at similar rates under plurality and RCV; 'none found that replacing FPTP with RCV disadvantages minority voters or candidates'; among 65+ just 6.5% prefer RCV to single vote; among Republicans under 7% vs 28% of Democrats; 'RCV alone likely cannot deliver the representational diversity that many advocates promise'; multi-seat districts produce more diverse representation; 'adopting RCV will not hurt as much as you might fear, but it may not help as much as you might hope'

Burnett and Kogan: more than 600,000 ballots in four local IRV elections; 'a substantial number of votes being discarded in each election'; 'the winner in all four of our cases receives less than a majority of the total votes cast'

Dowling et al. 2025: voter-file and Catalist data on local odd-year elections; RCV places not associated with lower turnout among people of color; several groups had higher turnout in RCV cities; largest proportional gains among White voters

McDaniel (SF State), San Francisco: RCV reduced turnout among infrequent voters; increased spoiled ballots concentrated in areas with more Black, Latino, elderly, foreign-born and less affluent residents, not fading over time; 'The ranking process is cognitively more difficult than just choosing one candidate'

Fair Representation Act (H.R. 4632, Beyer; cosponsors Raskin, Peters, McGovern, Khanna), introduced 23 July 2025: RCV for House and Senate; states with 6+ seats elect from 3-5 member districts, 5 or fewer at large; bars plans that materially favor a party and mid-decade redistricting except by court order; federal three-judge court draws maps if a state misses its deadline; House provisions after the 2030 census
